full_source_unit.source_text: Partials can exist without differentiability: $f=x_1x_2/(x_1^2+x_2^2)$, $f(0)=0$, has zero partials at $0$ but equals $\tfrac12$ on the diagonal; $C^1$ rules this out. "$C^1$ on a closed set $S$" means: the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open set containing $S$, so gradients exist on the boundary too.

A closed S contains its frontier. EqOn supplies exactly the source restriction values. No regularity of arbitrary other ambient completions or uniqueness across thin-set extensions is inferred.
scope_qualifications: The diagonal value1/2 is for t!=0, as required by the declared value f(0)=0. Both actual coordinate restrictions are identically zero; these are genuine derivative witnesses.
The explicit delta/4 diagonal point contradicts actual continuity at0; differentiability and C1 imply continuity and hence fail at0.

The closed-set C1 clause is the printed chosen open-neighborhood extension convention. The gradient is that chosen C1 extension at every S/frontier point; a different arbitrary ambient completion or uniqueness on a thin S is not asserted.
The boundary theorem requires S closed; the extension-gradient theorem works at all S points without needing closedness. Arbitrary finite coordinate sets I, including zero dimension, are covered.
